Content: A tropical storm is classified as major if it has sustained winds greater than `110` `text(miles per hour)`. Based on data from the past `text(two decades)`, a meteorologist estimated the following `text(percentages)` about future storms.

• `30%` of all tropical storms will originate in the eastern Pacific Ocean, of which `15%` will be classified as major.

• `50%` of all tropical storms will originate in the western Pacific Ocean, of which `25%` will be classified as major.
Based on the meteorologist's estimates, approximately what is the probability that a future tropical storm will originate in the Pacific Ocean and be classified as major?

What type of study was conducted, and what is the response variable of the study?

B.Choice: An experiment was conducted, and the response variable is the depth of the water.

D.Choice: An observational study was conducted, and the response variable is the concentration of the chemical.

Content: Ecologists wanted to estimate the mean biomass (amount of vegetation) of a certain forested region. The ecologists divided the region into plots measuring `1` `text(square meter)` each, and they selected a random sample of `9` plots. The mean biomass of the `9` plots was `4.3` `text(kilograms per square meter)` (`text(kg)//text(m)^2`) and the standard deviation was `1.5` `text(kg)//text(m)^2`. Staff members of a high school newspaper want to obtain an estimate of the average number of `text(years)` teachers in the state have been teaching. At an educational conference attended by many teachers in the state, the staff members randomly selected `50` conference attendees and asked the attendees how long they have been teaching. Which of the following describes the sample and the population to which it would be most reasonable for the staff members to generalize the results?

B.Choice: The sample is the `50` conference attendees, and the population is all conference attendees.

C.Choice: The sample is all conference attendees, and the population is all teachers in the state.

D.Choice: The sample is all conference attendees, and the population is the `50` conference attendees.

E.Choice: The sample is the average number of `text(years)` that all conference attendees have taught, and the population is all conference attendees.

Content: A `text(two-sided)` `t text(-test)` for a population mean is conducted of the null hypothesis `text(H)_0:mu=100`. Content: An agriculturalist working with Australian pine trees wanted to investigate the relationship between the age and the height of the Australian pine. A random sample of Australian pine trees was selected, and the age, in `text(years)`, and the height, in `text(meters)`, was recorded for `text(each tree)` in the sample. Based on the recorded data, the agriculturalist created the following regression equation to predict the height, in `text(meters)`, of the Australian pine based on the age, in `text(years)`, of the tree.
:ibox:predicted height `=0.29+0.48(text(age))`
Which of the following is the best interpretation of the slope of the regression line?

C.Choice: The height increases, on average, by `0.29` `text(meter each year)`.

D.Choice: The height increases, on average, by `0.29` `text(meter each 0.48 year)`.

E.Choice: The difference between the actual height and the predicted height is, on average, `0.48` `text(meter)` for `text(each year)`.

Content: At a certain store, the distribution of weights of cartons of large eggs is approximately normal with mean `26` `text(ounces)` (`text(oz)`). Based on the distribution, which of the following intervals will contain the greatest proportion of cartons of large eggs at the store?

Content: In `text(1960)` sociologists studied a random sample of `1text(,)018` families that consisted of a husband, a wife, and at least `text(one)` child. Of those families, `5.8` `text(percent)` reported that the wife was the primary wage earner of the family. Of those families, `22.3` `text(percent)` reported that the wife was the primary wage earner of the family. Which of the following represents a `99` `text(percent)` confidence interval for the difference between the proportions of families that consisted of a husband, a wife, and at least `text(one)` child from `text(1960)` to `text(2011)` that would have reported the wife as the primary wage earner?

Researchers working for a certain airline are investigating the weight of carry-on bags. The researchers will use the mean weight of a random sample of `800` carry-on bags to estimate the mean weight of all carry-on bags for the airline. Which of the following best describes the effect on the bias and the variance of the estimator if the researchers increase the sample size to `1text(,)300`?

B.Choice: The bias will increase and the variance will remain the same.

C.Choice: The bias will remain the same and the variance will decrease.

Content: Researchers investigated whether a new process for producing yarn could reduce the mean amount of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted by carpet. From random samples of carpets, the researchers found the mean reduction of VOCs emitted by carpets made with yarn produced by the new process compared with that of carpets made with yarn produced by the traditional process was `13` `text(parts per million)` (`text(ppm)`). All conditions for inference were met, and the `ptext(-value)` for the appropriate hypothesis test was `0.095`. Which of the following statements is the best interpretation of the `ptext(-value)`?

A.Choice: The probability that the null hypothesis is true is `0.095`.

B.Choice: The probability that the alternative hypothesis is true is `0.095`.

C.Choice: The probability of observing a mean reduction of `13` `text(ppm)` is `0.095`.

D.Choice: If the null hypothesis is true, the probability of observing a mean reduction of at least `13` `text(ppm)` is `0.095`.

E.Choice: If the null hypothesis is true, the probability of observing a mean reduction of at most `13` `text(ppm)` is `0.095`.

Content: A `99` `text(percent)` `text(one-sample)` `ztext(-interval)` for a proportion will be created from the point estimate obtained from each of `text(two)` random samples selected from the same population: sample `R` and sample `S`. Let `R` represent a random sample of size `1text(,)000`, and let `S` represent a random sample of size `4text(,)000`. If the point estimate obtained from `R` is equal to the point estimate obtained from `S`, which of the following must be true about the respective margins of error constructed from those samples?

B.Choice: The margin of error for `S` will be `2` times the margin of error for `R`.

D.Choice: The margin of error for `R` will be `4` times the margin of error for `S`.

Content: A study was conducted to evaluate the impact of taking a nutritional supplement on a person's reaction time. `text(One hundred)` volunteers were placed into `text(one)` of `text(three)` groups according to their athletic ability: low, moderate, or high. Content: Researchers believed that an increase in lean body mass is associated with an increase in maximal oxygen uptake. A scatterplot of the measurements taken from `18` randomly selected college athletes displayed a strong positive linear relationship between the `text(two)` variables. A significance test for the null hypothesis that the slope of the regression line is `0` versus the alternative that the slope is greater than `0` yielded a `ptext(-value)` of `0.04`. Which statement is an appropriate conclusion for the test?

A.Choice: The `ptext(-value)` of `0.04` indicates that `4%` of the variation in maximal oxygen uptake for college athletes can be explained by the amount of lean body mass.

B.Choice: The `ptext(-value)` of `0.04` indicates that `16%` of the variation in maximal oxygen uptake for college athletes can be explained by the amount of lean body mass.

C.Choice: The strong positive linear relationship displayed in the scatterplot along with a `ptext(-value)` less than `0.05` indicates that college athletes with higher lean body mass tend to have higher maximal oxygen uptake.

D.Choice: The strong positive linear relationship displayed in the scatterplot along with a `ptext(-value)` less than `0.05` indicates that an increase in lean body mass causes an increase in maximal oxygen uptake for college athletes.

E.Choice: A `ptext(-value)` less than `0.05` indicates that the relationship displayed in the scatterplot is likely due to chance, and that there is no statistical evidence of a relationship between lean body mass and maximal oxygen uptake for college athletes.

Content: An environmental group wanted to estimate the proportion of fresh produce sales identified as organic in a local grocery store. Content: In a standard golf tournament, golfers play `18` holes of golf on each of `4` consecutive `text(days)`. Content: Based on records kept at a gas station, the distribution of `text(gallons)` of gas purchased by customers is skewed to the right with mean `10` `text(gallons)` and standard deviation `4` `text(gallons)`. Content: A program that was intended to cure a person's fear of spiders was offered at a local zoo. Volunteers with a fear of spiders participated in the program, which included holding a spider for `15` `text(minutes)`. `text(One month)` after they completed the program, the participants were contacted and surveyed about the program. Over `90` `text(percent)` of the participants claimed they were cured of their fear of spiders. Based on the description of the program, which of the following statements is true?

A.Choice: Because over `90%` of the participants claimed to be cured, the results prove that holding a spider will cure a person's fear of spiders.

B.Choice: Because over `90%` of the participants claimed to be cured, the results can be generalized to the population of all people who have a fear of spiders.

C.Choice: Because the participants were volunteers, the study is a census of all people in the local area who have a fear of spiders.

D.Choice: Because the participants were self-selected, a person's desire to be cured could be a confounding variable.

E.Choice: Because participants held a spider for `15` `text(minutes)`, the study is an experiment and the results can be generalized to the population of all people who have a fear of spiders.

Content: A police officer uses a motion detector to indicate whether a car is traveling faster than the speed limit (speeding). A speeding ticket will be issued to the driver of the car if the officer believes the driver is speeding, as indicated by the detector. Content: An agricultural scientist wanted to compare the effect of a new fertilizer to that of `text(three)` older fertilizers — `text(X)`, `text(Y)`, and `text(Z)` — on the growth of vegetables typically grown in small gardens. `text(Two hundred)` green bean seedlings were individually planted in identical pots and randomly assigned to `text(one)` of `text(four)` groups of `50` each. At the end of `text(four weeks)`, all seedlings were dried and weighed. The scientist found that the mean weight of the seedlings in the group given the new fertilizer was significantly greater than the mean weights of seedlings in the other `text(three)` groups. The scientist concluded that the new fertilizer was more effective than the other fertilizers for all vegetables. Why is the scientist's conclusion `ultext(not)` appropriate?

A.Choice: The study was observational, so cause and effect cannot be concluded.

B.Choice: The study was observational, so no replication was used in the study.
